script.opening: “Hello doctor. I’ve had this cough for about three months now. The heart doctor said I should talk to you about it.”

facts.text: “Dry, tickly. All day, every day. Nothing comes up. It’s the same as when it started.”

facts.topic: When it started (if asked about timing or medicines)
facts.text: “Maybe a month after they put up my ramipril? I didn’t connect it.”
No coughing blood, no breathlessness, no wheeze, no chest pain, no fever, no weight loss, no night sweats, no hoarse voice, no swollen ankles, no trouble lying flat.
No heartburn or sour taste, no blocked or runny nose, no drip at the back of the throat, no asthma.
“No, never blacked out or felt faint when coughing.”

facts.topic: Driving and work (if asked about work or how the cough affects you)
facts.text: “I drive the number 42. When I get a coughing fit at the wheel, passengers stare. It’s embarrassing — and I worry about it.”

facts.topic: Missed doses (only if asked how you take your tablets or whether you ever miss any)
facts.text: Hesitate. “To be honest… on work days I’ve been leaving out the ramipril. About a month. I thought the cough was worse on days I took it. Please — will this get back to the DVLA?”
“I told them after the heart attack. They stopped me driving the bus, then I did a treadmill test and they gave it back four months ago.”
“Down from twenty to four a day — after work. It’s hard to stop the last few.” Interested in help if offered. Wife Laila wants you to stop.
If asked what you think: “My wife says it might be my lungs — her uncle had lung cancer and it started with a cough.”
Married to Laila; three adult children. Bus driver for 22 years. No alcohol. Walks 30 minutes most days since rehab.

Be calm and pleasant. Reveal the missed doses only if asked directly about how you take your tablets or about missing doses, and look embarrassed. If told to stop ramipril, ask: “Is that safe? The heart doctor said it protects my heart — I don’t want another heart attack.” Accept the switch if the reason is explained. If the doctor says the DVLA must be told about the missed doses, become anxious.

ice.ideas: “The cardiologist thought it was the cigarettes.”
ice.concerns: HIDDEN AGENDA — he has been missing ramipril on work days for a month because coughing fits at the wheel embarrass him and he worries about safety; he fears that admitting it will affect his bus licence. His wife fears lung cancer.
ice.expectations: To find out what is causing the cough and stop it — without endangering his heart or his job.

cues: “The heart doctor said to see you.” — the cardiologist attributed it to smoking without checking the medicines.
“Passengers stare.” — work impact, leading to the missed doses.
“My wife says it might be my lungs.” — a cancer worry to address.

checkpoints.text: Takes a cough history (onset, character, sputum, duration) and links timing to the ramipril dose increase; asks about other medicines and adherence

Screens for red flags and alternative causes: haemoptysis, weight loss, hoarseness, breathlessness, chest pain, heart failure symptoms, reflux, upper-airway symptoms, asthma; asks about cough syncope as a vocational driver
Discovers he has been omitting ramipril on work days and explores why; confirms DVLA notification and relicensing

Stops ramipril and switches to an ARB licensed after MI (for example valsartan, low dose titrated), with U&E, potassium and BP 1–2 weeks after starting and after dose increases; explains continuing secondary prevention
Arranges a chest X-ray within 2 weeks (NICE NG12: aged 40 or over, cough, ever smoked) and a review; explains expected resolution of ACE-inhibitor cough (usually 1–4 weeks, up to 3 months)
Supports stopping smoking completely (very brief advice, referral, NRT, varenicline or vaping) and safety-nets for chest pain, breathlessness, haemoptysis, blackouts or faintness at the wheel
Responds to the missed doses without judgement, explains that adherence problems are common and solvable, and clarifies honestly what the DVLA does and does not need to know
Addresses his fear of another heart attack and his wife’s fear of lung cancer, shares the plan and checks understanding

worked.txt: “When did the cough start, compared with any changes to your tablets?”
“Lots of people find it hard to take tablets that give them side effects. Are there any you’ve been leaving out, even sometimes?”
“Ramipril is well known for causing a dry, tickly cough in about one in ten people, often starting weeks or months after it’s begun or increased. That fits your story very well.”

“We won’t leave your heart unprotected. I’ll swap the ramipril for a close relative called valsartan, which protects the heart in a similar way but rarely causes a cough. We start low, check a blood test and your blood pressure in one to two weeks, and build it up.”
“Because you’ve smoked and the cough has lasted over three weeks, I’d like a chest X-ray in the next two weeks to be thorough — that’s also the answer to Laila’s worry.”

“The DVLA doesn’t need to know about the missed tablets — the key things are that your heart is stable and you haven’t blacked out. If you ever feel faint or black out with coughing, stop driving and tell us straight away.”

f.learning: A persistent dry cough in someone on an ACE inhibitor should prompt a medicines timeline: ACE-inhibitor cough affects around 1 in 10 people, can begin weeks or months after starting or increasing the dose, and usually settles within 1–4 weeks of stopping (occasionally up to 3 months). After myocardial infarction, NICE NG185 recommends an ACE inhibitor and, for people who are intolerant, an angiotensin-II receptor blocker instead — a switch that can be made safely in primary care with monitoring of renal function, potassium and BP. Do not let a probable drug cause close the differential: a man over 40 with a cough who has smoked meets NICE NG12 criteria for a chest X-ray within 2 weeks. Side effects often cause silent non-adherence, here driven by work; asking about missed doses in a normalising way protects secondary prevention. Vocational drivers raise specific DVLA questions — after acute coronary syndrome Group 2 relicensing depends on functional testing, and cough syncope is a separate driving issue — so ask about faintness with coughing and give honest information about what must be reported.

knowledge.guideline: NICE NG185 Acute coronary syndromes (2020) · NICE NG12 Suspected cancer: recognition and referral (2015) · DVLA — Assessing fitness to drive: a guide for medical professionals (current edition, accessed October 2026) · NICE NG209 Tobacco: preventing uptake, promoting quitting and treating dependence (2021)
knowledge.summary: Probable ACE-inhibitor cough: switch to an ARB licensed post-MI with monitoring, still request a 2-week chest X-ray, find and fix the missed doses, check cough syncope and DVLA status, and support complete smoking cessation.

points.t: Dry, tickly, non-productive; up to around 10% of users; onset hours to months after starting or a dose increase; not dose-dependent in a simple way; resolves usually within 1–4 weeks of stopping, sometimes up to 3 months. Re-challenge is not needed.

NICE NG185: offer an ARB instead if ACE-inhibitor intolerant. Valsartan is licensed after MI: usual adult dose — start 20 mg twice daily and titrate over several weeks towards 160 mg twice daily as tolerated (NICE NG185/SPC; check the SPC and local formulary; SPC: valsartan). Stop ramipril the day before starting. Check U&E, potassium and BP 1–2 weeks after starting and after each increase.

NICE NG12: offer an urgent chest X-ray (within 2 weeks) to people aged 40 and over with unexplained cough (or other listed symptoms) who have ever smoked. A normal X-ray with resolution after stopping the ACE inhibitor completes the picture; persistent cough needs further assessment.
Smoking, asthma or COPD, gastro-oesophageal reflux, upper-airway cough syndrome, heart failure (orthopnoea, oedema), lung cancer, interstitial lung disease, infection including TB.

Group 2 drivers after ACS must not drive until relicensed by the DVLA, which requires functional testing. Cough syncope: Group 2 drivers should not drive and must notify the DVLA — ask directly about faintness or blackouts with cough. Missed doses themselves are not notifiable.

ACE inhibitor or ARB, beta-blocker, aspirin lifelong plus a second antiplatelet for up to 12 months, high-intensity statin, cardiac rehabilitation, complete smoking cessation (NICE NG209: behavioural support plus varenicline, NRT or nicotine vaping).
The Clear pass candidate links the cough to the dose increase, still does the X-ray, finds the missed doses with a non-judgemental question, and gives accurate, reassuring DVLA information.

model.text: Hello Mr Karimi, I’m Dr Evans. Can you see and hear me? I’ve read the heart clinic letter — tell me about the cough.
Dry and tickly, three months, all day. Nothing comes up.
Any blood, weight loss, hoarse voice, breathlessness, wheeze, chest pain, swollen ankles, or trouble lying flat?
Heartburn, a blocked nose or a drip at the back of your throat? And have you ever felt faint or blacked out when coughing?
When did it start compared with any tablet changes? And lots of people find tablets hard to take — are there any you sometimes leave out?
model.why: Medicines timeline and normalised adherence question

model.text: About a month after they upped the ramipril. And… I’ve been leaving the ramipril out on work days. The coughing at the wheel — passengers stare. Will this get back to the DVLA?
Thank you for telling me — that took courage, and it really helps. Missed tablets aren’t something the DVLA needs to know. Have you told them about the heart attack?
model.why: Non-judgemental; honest DVLA information; checks status

model.text: Yes — I did the treadmill test and got my licence back four months ago.
I think the ramipril is causing the cough. It does this in about one in ten people, often after a dose increase. The good news is we can switch it.
Is that safe? The heart doctor said it protects my heart.

It does — so we won’t stop protection. I’ll swap it for valsartan, which protects the heart in a similar way but rarely causes a cough. Stop the ramipril today and start valsartan tomorrow — every day, work days too. We’ll check a blood test and your blood pressure in one to two weeks and build up the dose.
model.why: Safe switch with monitoring and adherence plan

model.text: Because you’ve smoked and the cough has lasted a while, I’d also like a chest X-ray in the next two weeks — to be thorough. Is there anything you or Laila are worried it might be?
Laila thinks it’s my lungs — her uncle had cancer.

That’s an understandable worry, and the X-ray will help answer it. The cough should start easing within a few weeks of stopping ramipril, though it can take up to three months. You’ve done brilliantly cutting to four a day — would you like help to stop the last few? That’s the biggest thing for your heart and lungs now.
model.why: Addresses the wife’s fear; smoking support

model.text: If you get chest pain, breathlessness, cough up blood, or feel faint or black out — especially driving — stop and get help: 999 for chest pain. What’s the plan in your words?
Stop ramipril, start valsartan tomorrow every day, blood test in two weeks, X-ray, and see the stop smoking people.

social.t: Visible side effects at work (coughing at the wheel) drive silent non-adherence; ask about work impact.
Partners’ fears (lung cancer) shape what patients accept; addressing them helps adherence to the plan.

legal.t: The licence holder must notify relevant conditions; doctors advise and, if a patient continues to drive unsafely despite advice, may disclose to the DVLA (GMC confidentiality guidance, 2017). Missed doses are not notifiable; cough syncope is.

professional.t: Specialist letters can attribute symptoms without a medicines review; the GP holds the full timeline. Switching ACE inhibitor to ARB does not need cardiology approval.

community.t: NHS Stop Smoking Service; community pharmacy (New Medicine Service for the valsartan start); British Heart Foundation information.

redFlags: Faintness or syncope with coughing (vocational driver)
ice: Concern: missed doses and licence; wife fears cancer
core: Ramipril increased 4 months ago; cough 1 month later

playbook.diagnosis: Probable ACE-inhibitor (ramipril) induced cough, with intermittent non-adherence; chest X-ray needed to exclude lung pathology in a smoker over 40.
playbook.diagnosisLay: “The ramipril is the most likely cause of your cough. We can swap it for a similar heart-protecting tablet that rarely causes a cough — and do an X-ray to be thorough.”

management.reflectIce: “You were worried that leaving out the ramipril might cost you your licence, and Laila worries about your lungs. The DVLA doesn’t need to know about missed tablets, the switch keeps your heart protected, and the X-ray will answer Laila’s question.”
management.psychosocial: Daily dosing that suits shift patterns; involve Laila; praise smoking progress.
sharedPlan: Stop ramipril; start valsartan next day (start low, titrate)
U&E, potassium and BP at 1–2 weeks and after each dose increase
Review with X-ray and bloods in 2 weeks
safetyNet: Faintness or blackout with cough — stop driving and contact us
Cough not improving by 3 months or new symptoms — review

pitfalls.intro: The cardiology letter points to smoking; candidates who follow it, or who stop at the ACE inhibitor, both fail.

items.fail: Accepts “smoking-related” and never builds a medicines timeline.
items.why: The ramipril increase a month before the cough is the clue in the record.
items.fix: Ask when the cough started relative to any medicine changes.

items.fail: Diagnoses ACE-inhibitor cough and does not request a chest X-ray.
items.why: NICE NG12 recommends a chest X-ray within 2 weeks for a smoker over 40 with cough — drug cough and cancer can coexist.
items.fix: Switch the drug and request the X-ray.

items.fail: Reacts to the missed doses with a warning about another heart attack, or says the DVLA must be told.
items.why: Judgement shuts down disclosure; the DVLA information is wrong and frightens him.
items.fix: Thank him, explain the switch removes the reason to miss doses, and give accurate DVLA advice including cough syncope.

timeMap.d: Use the cardiology letter; open question.
Cough, red flags, alternatives, cough syncope; medicines timeline; adherence; DVLA.
ACE-inhibitor cough; valsartan with monitoring; daily on work days.
NG12 chest X-ray; wife’s worry; complete cessation support.

wordPics.clearFail: Attributes the cough to smoking, offers a linctus, or stops ramipril without a replacement; no X-ray; missed doses never found.
wordPics.fail: Switches to an ARB appropriately but omits monitoring or the chest X-ray, or misses the adherence problem, or gives wrong DVLA information.
wordPics.pass: Medicines timeline; red flags and cough syncope; switches to a post-MI ARB with U&E and BP checks; chest X-ray within 2 weeks; finds missed doses; smoking support; safety-net.
wordPics.clearPass: All of the Pass, with a normalising adherence question, accurate DVLA reassurance, explicit plan for work-day dosing, both the patient’s and his wife’s worries addressed, and teach-back.

avoid.dont: “It’s probably the smoking — try to stop.”
avoid.instead: “When did the cough start compared with any tablet changes?”

avoid.dont: “You must take your tablets or you’ll have another heart attack.”
avoid.instead: “Lots of people miss tablets that cause side effects — let’s switch to one that suits you.”

avoid.dont: “It’s definitely the ramipril — no need for tests.”
avoid.instead: “The ramipril is the likely cause, and I’d still like a chest X-ray to be thorough.”
